messages.subject: Re: Removing the correlation parameter
messages.body_plain:
Hi Zhenguang, 

I don't have time to give more than a quick reply, but what you are seeing is some weirdness with how variables defined as data type "factor" behave in regression models. You seem to have four levels of Prime, and if you remove the correlations between the levels you should have three slopes.  So, neither syntax is giving you the right answer!  What you can do in this case is just explicitly define three separate dummy variables, eg.  PrimeC, PrimeE, PrimeF, and then explicitly spell out (0 + PrimeC | Subject) + (0 + PrimeE | Subject) etc.. 

-Dale

Sent from Samsung Mobile

From: Zhenguang Cai <zhenguangcai at gmail.com>

Subject: [R-lang]  Removing the correlation parameter 
 
Hi all,

Barr et al. (2013) recommended a design-driven (i.e., maximal random 
structure) approach for LME. However, as some of you may have 
experienced, LME with maximal random structure on categorical data would 
often result in non-convergence. Barr et al. recommended, in these 
cases, removing the correlation parameter (i.e., correlation between a 
random intercept and the corresponding random slope). However, I found 
that Barr et al. (e.g., p.262, Table 1) and Baayen et al. (2008, p.395) 
used different R scripts to do this. I wonder which is the correct way 
to do. I use my own example below.

Barr et al: (But still correlations between levels of the fixed 
predictor in the results)
Generalized linear mixed model fit by the Laplace approximation
Formula: ResponseC ~ Prime + (1 | Subject) + (0 + Prime | Subject) + (1 
|      Item) + (0 + Prime | Item)

  Item    (Intercept) 2.7090e+00 1.6459e+00
Number of obs: 720, groups: Subject, 35; Item, 24

Fixed effects:

messages.subject: Re: Removing the correlation parameter
messages.body_plain:
Hi Garry,
 
There's a few ways you could convert your single factor into multiple dummy coded variables. The quickest way I can think of right now would be to do:
 
E1$PrimeE <- as.factor(ifelse(E1$Prime=="E",1,0))
E1$PrimeF <- as.factor(ifelse(E1$Prime=="F",1,0))
 
Then, as Dale suggested, you would use: ... + (0 + PrimeE) + (0 + PrimeF) + ...
 
PrimeC would be when both PrimeE and PrimeF were 0. So the intercept would have the same meaning in the fixed effects.
 
HTH,
 
Ian

messages.subject: Re: Removing the correlation parameter
messages.body_plain:
Hi Garry et al.,

Just a couple of follow-ups:

1) I generally agree with Dale & Ian's suggestions, but note that we used sum (or "deviation") coding, *not* dummy coding, in Barr et al.  As we wrote in that paper, when you remove correlation parameters, the way you set up your contrasts affects model class, and in general dummy and treatment coding will work a bit worse than sum coding in terms of controlling Type I error.

   In that paper we didn't deal with factors of more than two levels, and I haven't looked at that situation carefully.  My intuition is that sum coding would also be better than dummy coding for this situation, but I'm not really that sure.  It'd be worth it for someone to do simulations to test this. I'm also not sure whether performance will be independent of choice of baseline factor level in this situation.

2) The Baayen et al. type random effects structure:

     (I)  (1 | Subject) + (1 | Prime:Subject)

   leads to a different model than the one that Dale and Ian suggested.  Note that Baayen et al say they are simplifying [the random slopes model] "by removing the correlation parameter and by assuming homoskedasticity for the subjects with respect to the SOA conditions".  Technically speaking, model (I) does not entirely remove correlation between subject-specific responses to each condition: doing this and also assuming homoskedasticity would be achieved by the model:

    (II)  (1 | Prime:Subject)

   Rather, model (I) has assumed homoskedasticity across Prime conditions for subjects, and constrained the between-condition correlation to be between 0 (which would happen when the (1 | Subject) variance is 0) and +1 (which would happen when the (1 | Prime:Subject) variance is 0).

   If what I just said doesn't make sense, then I *strongly* recommend that you work through the math behind the models before trying to use model (I), feeling free to ask follow-up questions.

   At any rate, I generally use the Barr et al. style approach to removing random slopes, but I think that models (I) and (II) are also reasonable models and should tend to work fairly well.  In terms of testing within-group fixed effects, they'll probably behave pretty similarly to what Ian's suggesting (random slopes for dummy-coded versions of the predictors) -- not bad, but a bit more anti-conservative than sum-coding.

Best & hope this helps,

Roger

messages.body_plain:
Dear Zhenuang,

Let me just add that --if you have a hypothesis over orders of the four levels of prime (a common case)-- I'd use Helmert coding. See Maureen Gillespie's tutorial on coding categorical predictors.

You can also define three Helmert coded predictor variables and then remove slopes or random correlations as necessary. 

Finally, I wouldn't worry too much about the effect of helmet vs sum vs treatment coding on type I errors. Those problems are probably going to be tiny in comparison to type I error inflation due to eg trying multiple codings or trying various covariates (and then only reporting significant results).

Florian

Hi Hao,

> Given ten count numbers (1,7,16,13,11,11,12,10,8,4),

> (a) the biggest (i.e. 16) and is significantly  higher than other
> values
> (b) the top two values as a group (16 and 13) is significantly  higher
> than other values

Could you tell us a little more about the setup here? What are the
values? What hypothesis are you trying to test? How did you gather the
data?

By "significantly higher than the other values" do you mean
"significantly higher than the mean"? (Or do you mean "higher than the
second-highest value"?) Seeing if the highest is far from the mean could 
potentially be a nonsensical comparison because if you have enough data 
points you will necessarily have some far from the mean under any 
reasonable null hypothesis. On the other hand, there are tests for 
whether or not a data set contains any outliers (further from the mean 
than what I would expect, given my sample size), which may be what you want. 

So it would be helpful for you to tell us more about your data setup and
what you're trying to determine. 

Best,

++Steve

On 09/08/13 05:27, Hao Wang wrote:
> Hi Steve,
> 
> Many thanks for your response.
> 
> The ten numbers are from a counting process in the interval (0,1). The interval
> (0,1) is partitioned into 10  sub-intervals (0,0.1), (0.1,0.2),...,(0.9,1).
> The values are the number of events (in my case, DNA mutations) happened in
> each interval. Now 16, the value in (0.2, 0.3) is the highest value among
> the ten. I want to know if mutation hotspot exists here, so I want to test
> if this value is significantly higher than other values. It would be good
> to take other values as a group and the highest value or the top-two values
> as another group and test whether the two groups have significantly
> different mutation number.

This might not be what you want, but one way of rephrasing your question
is to ask what the chances are of finding 16 or more DNA mutations in
one of 10 bins (given a null hypothesis that mutations will be equally
distributed across bins).  This kind of question is easily answered
using a bit of simulation.  For example, below is a function in R which
randomly allocates 93 events to one of 10 bins, and then returns 1 if
one of those bins includes 16 or more events (or zero otherwise).  By
calling the function repeatedly we can find the proportion of trials in
which there are 16 or more events in a single bin (or in other words,
the probability of finding 16 events in a bin purely by chance).

The last line below runs the code 10,000 times to estimate the relevant
probability.  As you will see if you run the code yourself, it's roughly
.2; or, there is a 1 in 5 chance of finding 16 entries in a sub-interval
even if there's no mutation hotspot, so there's probably no reason to
suspect that there's anything "special" about (0.2, 0.3) (sorry!).

Code follows:  Someone on the list can point to any errors (and
doubtless provide a more elegant version :) ).

=========== snip

total <- sum(1,7,16,13,11,11,12,10,8,4)
runs <- 10000


one.run <- function(found=16,samp.size=total,bins=10) {
  x <- rle(sort(sample(1:bins,size=samp.size,replace=T)))
  rv <- 0
  if (max(x$lengths) >= found) { rv <- 1}
  return (rv)
}

sum(replicate(runs,one.run(found=16))) / run

=========== snip

--MC

total <- sum(1,7,16,13,11,11,12,10,8,4)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Hao,

> Subsequently, I want to know If there is a proper test that can do
> contrast between two groups of counting numbers? Or if this is a valid
> question? 

I think the real challenge you have is not of doing an statistical test
on counts. It's that your selection criterion for which intervals to
compare (16 in 0.2-0.3, vs all others) is NOT independent of the thing
you are measuring (the count). This makes it problematic/nonsensical to
use most standard statistical tests because they assume independence.
You could not, for instance, just do a nonparametric test on 16 vs. all
the others, because you used the extreme-ness of 16 to pick it as the
comparison, which violates the assumptions of the test. So even though
it would print out a test statistic and p value, they wouldn't actually
represent anything meaningful.

This is why its useful to think in detail about the simulation Martin
sent, or to consider tests like outlier tests that determine if, in
aggregate, there is an outlier in the data. Another approach you might
consider is that of making your selection criteria of which bin to test,
and the data you choose to test it actually independent. You could do
this by using, say, 1/2 of the data to choose which bin you *think* is
largest, and then testing its count data from the second half of the
data, versus the mean of the rest on the second half. That way, your
selection of bins is statistically independent of the data you analyze
(under the null hypothesis) because they occur on different subsets of
the data. I'm pretty sure, though, that on the example you sent, you'll
get very similar results to Martin's simulation with any
approach--probably nothing so special about 16. It's less than 2 SDs
from the mean of even the other data, after all.

++Steve

> it would print out a test statistic and p value, they wouldn't actually
> represent anything meaningful.
>
> This is why its useful to think in detail about the simulation Martin
> sent, or to consider tests like outlier tests that determine if, in
> aggregate, there is an outlier in the data. Another approach you might
> consider is that of making your selection criteria of which bin to test,
> and the data you choose to test it actually independent. You could do
> this by using, say, 1/2 of the data to choose which bin you *think* is
> largest, and then testing its count data from the second half of the
> data, versus the mean of the rest on the second half. That way, your
> selection of bins is statistically independent of the data you analyze
> (under the null hypothesis) because they occur on different subsets of
> the data. I'm pretty sure, though, that on the example you sent, you'll
> get very similar results to Martin's simulation with any
> approach--probably nothing so special about 16. It's less than 2 SDs
> from the mean of even the other data, after all.
>
> ++Steve
>
>
>

Dear Steve,

Perhaps it's going a bit too far to say the use of a standard test is
"nonsensical" here. I compared a chi-squared test (with Bonferroni
correction) with a simulation approach, and got a reasonably close answer,
p = 0.206 vs. p = 0.209.

---

total <- 93

high <- 16

bins <- 10

reps <- 100000

set.seed(1)


chisq.test(c(high, total - high), p = c(1 / bins, (1 - 1 / bins)))$p.value *bins

# 0.2056598


hit <- vector()

for (i in 1:reps){

v <- sample(1:bins, total, replace = T)

if (max(table(v)) >= high)

hit[i] <- 1

else

hit[i] <- 0}

mean(hit)

# 0.2088

messages.subject: negative deviances under more realistic circumstances
messages.subject_clean: negative deviances under more realistic circumstances
messages.body_plain:
Like Florian Jaeger in a thread awhile back, I've encountered negative  
deviances in fitting linear mixed effects models. They arose while  
comparing two different ways of excluding outliers. The baseline model  
includes all 10693 observations (from 21 participants), the second  
excludes observations faster and slower than the 0.05-99.5 percentiles  
of the log RTs (10585 observations remaining), and the third excludes  
observations faster and slower than the median RT -/+ 4 MAD median  
absolute deviations (10540 observations). All three models include the  
same six fixed effects (all independent) and one random effect, by  
participant. All produce very similar parameter estimates for the  
fixed effects and only slightly different residual variances:

All observations:              6.6939e-02
Excluding 0.5-99.5 percentile  5.7860e-02
Excluding -/+ 4 MAD:           5.5922e-02

so the residual standard deviations don't differ much.

The log likelihoods and deviances differ between the first two models  
in the expected direction:

                                -2LL    deviance  REML deviance
All observations:              -887.5  1705      1775
Excluding 0.5-99.5 percentile  -107.6  143.6     215.2

but for the third model they have opposite signs from what I expected:

                                -2LL    deviance  REML deviance
Excluding -/+ 4 MAD:           72.86   -217.6    -145.7

The AIC value for this model is also negative, -73.73, cf. 1847 and  
287.2 for the all observations and 0.5-99.5 models.

I know that negative deviances are possible but they're surprising  
with this data set, given the residual variances and standard  
deviations aren't that different or small. One possible hint has to do  
with the relationship between the MAD and the standard deviation of  
the log RTs:

MAD = 0.1921519 (median = 6.740941)
sd = 0.3029887 (mean = 6.777124)

The sd is somewhat larger than the value predicted from the MAD if the  
data were normally distributed, namely:

1.4826 * MAD = 0.2848843

but then test of the normality of the log RT distribution definitively  
showed that they aren't normally distributed (Anderson-Darling: A =  
60.3473,  p < 2.2e-16 and Lilliefors (= Kolmogorov-Smirnov) D =  
0.0516, p < 2.2e-16). QQ-plots show that the log transform does make  
the distribution closer to normal, but the normal distribution still  
underestimates the number of responses faster than the mean RT and  
overestimates the number slower than the mean. I haven't attached  
these plots because I'm not sure this listserv accepts mail with  
attachments. If anyone wants to see them or anything else about the  
data, just let me know.

So, after this long preamble, I have a pair of simple questions:  
should I be surprised at getting negative deviances, and have I made a  
mistake? Thanks.


John Kingston

messages.subject: Re: negative deviances under more realistic circumstances

messages.body_plain:
The negative deviances (and negative AIC and positive logLik) basically
just mean the estimated likelihood function is very narrow.  This is not
necessarily a sign of anything wrong.  I think what would worry me more if
I were you is how much your model seems to be changing given the relatively
small differences in exclusions.  It looks like the MAD exclusion is
excluding just under 1.5% of your data, and the 0.5-99.5 exclusion is
around 1%, but the changes in model fit look pretty big to me.  You may
want to double- and triple-check your exclusion procedure, and graph some
things to see if the outliers are hugely outlying or something, or if
you're changing the transformation of any variables between the models
(like re-standardizing after exclusions or something).  But as long as
you're doing what you think you're doing, and the data doesn't look
horribly weird in some way (a little non-normality shouldn't be a big deal)
there should be no problems with the negative deviances (positive log
likelihoods).

So in short, spend your thought and energy directed towards why your model
fit seems to be changing so much by excluding relatively little data, and
if that all makes sense (e.g., you're getting rid of some truly heinous
outliers), then don't sweat the negative deviances.

my two cents,
-scott
